claims.text: High aggregate accuracy can hide systematic errors in rare subclasses.
claims.poster_quote: High aggregate accuracy can hide systematic errors in rare subclasses.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: high aggregate accuracy is a stable property of both architectures. Despite this overall stability, errors cluster in specific low-frequency subclasses
claims.reason: Section 6.1 and 6.2 describe how high aggregate accuracy (97%+) conceals systematic errors in rare subclasses like Type 4-2.

claims.text: Dataset statistics exclude canonical Type 3 irregulars.
claims.poster_quote: Dataset statistics exclude canonical Type 3 irregulars �� and ��.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Canonical irregular verbs (する, くる; Type 3) and polysemous lemmas with multiple inflected forms are excluded to maintain a one-to-one lemma–form mapping.
claims.reason: Section 3.1 explicitly states that Type 3 irregulars are excluded from the dataset.

claims.text: Type 4-2 is 0.9% of data.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2 is 0.9% of data, yet causes 30.2% and 43.1% of PGT and LST errors, respectively.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 (/e/ + gemination, e.g. あきれかえる akirekaeru → あきれかえった akirekaetta). Count: 37. Prop. (%): 0.9
claims.reason: Table 1 confirms that Type 4-2 constitutes 0.9% of the dataset.

claims.text: Type 4-2 causes 30.2% of PGT errors.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2 is 0.9% of data, yet causes 30.2% and 43.1% of PGT and LST errors, respectively.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 verbs are massively overrepresented, accounting for 30.2% (PGT) ... of all errors while comprising just 0.9% of the dataset.
claims.reason: Table 4 and Section 6.4 explicitly state that Type 4-2 accounts for 30.2% of PGT errors.

claims.text: Type 4-2 causes 43.1% of LST errors.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2 is 0.9% of data, yet causes 30.2% and 43.1% of PGT and LST errors, respectively.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 verbs are massively overrepresented, accounting for ... 43.1% (LST) of all errors while comprising just 0.9% of the dataset.
claims.reason: Table 4 and Section 6.4 explicitly state that Type 4-2 accounts for 43.1% of LST errors.

claims.text: Type 4-2 error rates are 43% for PGT.
claims.poster_quote: Its error rates are 43% and 60%, over 70 times the Type 1 rate.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 shows an error rate of 43% (PGT) ... more than 70 times the rate of Type 1 verbs.
claims.reason: Figure 1 and Section 6.4 confirm the 43% error rate for Type 4-2 in PGT.

claims.text: Type 4-2 error rates are 60% for LST.
claims.poster_quote: Its error rates are 43% and 60%, over 70 times the Type 1 rate.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 shows an error rate of ... 60% (LST), more than 70 times the rate of Type 1 verbs.
claims.reason: Figure 1 and Section 6.4 confirm the 60% error rate for Type 4-2 in LST.

claims.text: Type 4-2 error rates are over 70 times the Type 1 rate.
claims.poster_quote: Its error rates are 43% and 60%, over 70 times the Type 1 rate.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 shows an error rate of 43% (PGT) and 60% (LST), more than 70 times the rate of Type 1 verbs.
claims.reason: Figure 1 and Section 6.4 confirm that Type 4-2 error rates are over 70 times the Type 1 rate.

claims.text: Disparity Ratios for Type 4-2 reach 33.6 for PGT.
claims.poster_quote: Disparity Ratios reach 33.6 and 47.9; Type 4-1 trails at 8.17 and 3.93.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 contributes 34–48× its proportional representation to total errors ... DRg = Error Shareg / Data Shareg ... DR (PGT): 33.6
claims.reason: Table 5 and Figure 2 confirm that the Disparity Ratio for Type 4-2 in PGT is 33.6.

claims.text: Disparity Ratios for Type 4-2 reach 47.9 for LST.
claims.poster_quote: Disparity Ratios reach 33.6 and 47.9; Type 4-1 trails at 8.17 and 3.93.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 contributes 34–48× its proportional representation to total errors ... DRg = Error Shareg / Data Shareg ... DR (LST): 47.9
claims.reason: Table 5 and Figure 2 confirm that the Disparity Ratio for Type 4-2 in LST is 47.9.

claims.text: Disparity Ratios for Type 4-1 are 8.17 for PGT.
claims.poster_quote: Disparity Ratios reach 33.6 and 47.9; Type 4-1 trails at 8.17 and 3.93.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: DRg = Error Shareg / Data Shareg ... DR (PGT): 8.17
claims.reason: Table 5 confirms that the Disparity Ratio for Type 4-1 in PGT is 8.17.

claims.text: Disparity Ratios for Type 4-1 are 3.93 for LST.
claims.poster_quote: Disparity Ratios reach 33.6 and 47.9; Type 4-1 trails at 8.17 and 3.93.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: DRg = Error Shareg / Data Shareg ... DR (LST): 3.93
claims.reason: Table 5 confirms that the Disparity Ratio for Type 4-1 in LST is 3.93.

claims.text: Types 1 and 2 remain below 1 in Disparity Ratios.
claims.poster_quote: Types 1 and 2 remain below 1, while exact tests reject prevalence-only explanations across both architectures.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: DRg = Error Shareg / Data Shareg ... DR (PGT): 0.45 (Type 1), 0.52 (Type 2) ... DR (LST): 0.40 (Type 1), 0.60 (Type 2)
claims.reason: Table 5 confirms that Disparity Ratios for Types 1 and 2 are below 1 for both PGT and LST.

claims.text: Exact tests reject prevalence-only explanations across both architectures.
claims.poster_quote: Types 1 and 2 remain below 1, while exact tests reject prevalence-only explanations across both architectures.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: A one-sided exact binomial test rejects this null decisively for both systems (PGT: 16/53 errors, p = 3.6 × 10−20 ; LST: 22/51 errors, p = 2.7 × 10−31 ).
claims.reason: Section 6.4 explicitly states that exact tests reject the null hypothesis of prevalence-only error distribution for both architectures.

claims.text: Removing Type 4-2 beats removing all irregular verbs in improving accuracy.
claims.poster_quote: Removing it beats removing all irregular verbs, so evaluation should report subgroup performance and error concentration.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the LST system, removing only Type 4-2 yields the largest observed gain ... The gain is substantially larger than removing all irregular verbs.
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 6 confirm that removing Type 4-2 improves accuracy more than removing all irregular verbs.

claims.text: Evaluation should report subgroup performance and error concentration.
claims.poster_quote: Removing it beats removing all irregular verbs, so evaluation should report subgroup performance and error concentration.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Evaluation protocols ... may therefore benefit from subgroup-aware diagnostics of the kind proposed here, and not aggregate accuracy alone.
claims.reason: Section 7 explicitly argues for reporting subgroup performance and error concentration.

claims.text: The Pointer-Generator Transformer (PGT) copies from and attends to the lemma.
claims.poster_quote: The Pointer-Generator Transformer (PGT) copies from and attends to the lemma.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Pointer-Generator Transformer (henceforth PGT), incorporating a pointer-generator copying mechanism (See et al., 2017) with attention over the input lemma.
claims.reason: Section 4 describes the PGT architecture as copying from and attending to the lemma.

claims.text: The Lemma-Split Transformer (LST) prevents train–test lemma overlap.
claims.poster_quote: The Lemma-Split Transformer (LST) prevents train–test lemma overlap, testing unseen-lemma generalization.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Lemma-Split Transformer (henceforth LST) ... uses a lemma-split training and evaluation regime, preventing a lemma from appearing in both training and test data.
claims.reason: Section 4 describes the LST as preventing train–test lemma overlap.

claims.text: Both PGT and LST generate autoregressively using cross-entropy and teacher forcing.
claims.poster_quote: Both generate autoregressively using cross-entropy and teacher forcing.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Both models are trained with cross-entropy loss and teacher forcing, using the default hyperparameter configurations from their respective shared-task baselines.
claims.reason: Section 5.1 confirms that both PGT and LST use cross-entropy and teacher forcing.

claims.text: Across five seeds, both models make 104 errors spanning six failure modes.
claims.poster_quote: Across five seeds, both models make 104 errors spanning six failure modes.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Aggregated across five seeds, we observe 104 total errors, 53 from the PGT system and 51 from the LST system.
claims.reason: Section 6.3 explicitly states that both models make 104 errors across five seeds.

claims.text: PGT makes 53 errors.
claims.poster_quote: PGT makes 53 errors; LST makes 51 errors.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Aggregated across five seeds, we observe ... 53 from the PGT system.
claims.reason: Section 6.3 explicitly states that PGT makes 53 errors.

claims.text: LST makes 51 errors.
claims.poster_quote: PGT makes 53 errors; LST makes 51 errors.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Aggregated across five seeds, we observe ... 51 from the LST system.
claims.reason: Section 6.3 explicitly states that LST makes 51 errors.

claims.text: Gemination failures dominate 75.5% of PGT errors.
claims.poster_quote: Gemination failures dominate: 75.5% of PGT errors and 80.3% of LST errors.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Gemination-related errors (omission and insertion combined) dominate residual failures, accounting for 75.5% (PGT) ... of all errors.
claims.reason: Section 6.3 explicitly states that gemination failures dominate 75.5% of PGT errors.

claims.text: Gemination failures dominate 80.3% of LST errors.
claims.poster_quote: Gemination failures dominate: 75.5% of PGT errors and 80.3% of LST errors.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Gemination-related errors (omission and insertion combined) dominate residual failures, accounting for ... 80.3% (LST) of all errors.
claims.reason: Section 6.3 explicitly states that gemination failures dominate 80.3% of LST errors.

claims.text: 33 PGT errors are gemination omissions.
claims.poster_quote: 33 PGT and 32 LST errors are gemination omissions, especially missing required � after stem-final /e/ in Type 4-2.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Gemination-related errors ... omissions far more frequent than insertions in both systems ... 33 (62.3%) [PGT].
claims.reason: Table 3 confirms that PGT makes 33 gemination omission errors.

claims.text: 32 LST errors are gemination omissions.
claims.poster_quote: 33 PGT and 32 LST errors are gemination omissions, especially missing required � after stem-final /e/ in Type 4-2.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Gemination-related errors ... omissions far more frequent than insertions in both systems ... 32 (62.7%) [LST].
claims.reason: Table 3 confirms that LST makes 32 gemination omission errors.

claims.text: Gemination omissions especially involve missing required � after stem-final /e/ in Type 4-2.
claims.poster_quote: 33 PGT and 32 LST errors are gemination omissions, especially missing required � after stem-final /e/ in Type 4-2.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The dominant Type 4-2 failure is omission of required gemination before a stem-final /e/, e.g. あきれかえった akirekaetta → あきれかえた akirekaeta.
claims.reason: Section 6.6 explicitly states that gemination omissions especially involve missing required っ after stem-final /e/ in Type 4-2.

claims.text: Gemination insertions add 7 PGT errors.
claims.poster_quote: Gemination insertions add 7 PGT and 9 LST errors, mainly spurious � in Type 2.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Gemination-related errors ... insertions ... 7 (13.2%) [PGT].
claims.reason: Table 3 confirms that PGT makes 7 gemination insertion errors.

claims.text: Gemination insertions add 9 LST errors.
claims.poster_quote: Gemination insertions add 7 PGT and 9 LST errors, mainly spurious � in Type 2.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Gemination-related errors ... insertions ... 9 (17.6%) [LST].
claims.reason: Table 3 confirms that LST makes 9 gemination insertion errors.

claims.text: Gemination insertions mainly involve spurious � in Type 2.
claims.poster_quote: Gemination insertions add 7 PGT and 9 LST errors, mainly spurious � in Type 2.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Spurious gemination insertion occurs mainly in Type 2 verbs, e.g. おきた okita → おきった okitta.
claims.reason: Section 6.6 explicitly states that gemination insertions mainly involve spurious っ in Type 2.

claims.text: Removing Type 4-2 yields the largest single-subtype accuracy gain in both systems.
claims.poster_quote: Removing Type 4-2 yields the largest single-subtype accuracy gain in both systems.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the LST system, removing only Type 4-2 yields the largest observed gain ... For the PGT system, removing Type 4-2 alone is still the single best condition.
claims.reason: Section 6.7 confirms that removing Type 4-2 yields the largest single-subtype accuracy gain in both systems.

claims.text: LST accuracy rises from 97.73% to 99.75% after removing Type 4-2.
claims.poster_quote: LST rises from 97.73% to 99.75%: a 2.02-point gain and approximately 89% error reduction, versus a 1.22-point gain after removing all irregulars.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the LST system, removing only Type 4-2 yields the largest observed gain: 97.73% → 99.75%.
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 7 confirm that LST accuracy rises from 97.73% to 99.75% after removing Type 4-2.

claims.text: LST accuracy gain after removing Type 4-2 is 2.02 points.
claims.poster_quote: LST rises from 97.73% to 99.75%: a 2.02-point gain and approximately 89% error reduction, versus a 1.22-point gain after removing all irregulars.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the LST system, removing only Type 4-2 yields the largest observed gain: 97.73% → 99.75% (+2.02).
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 6 confirm that the LST accuracy gain after removing Type 4-2 is 2.02 points.

claims.text: LST error reduction after removing Type 4-2 is approximately 89%.
claims.poster_quote: LST rises from 97.73% to 99.75%: a 2.02-point gain and approximately 89% error reduction, versus a 1.22-point gain after removing all irregulars.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the LST system, removing only Type 4-2 yields the largest observed gain: 97.73% → 99.75% (+2.02), corresponding to an approximately 89% reduction in error rate.
claims.reason: Section 6.7 explicitly states that the LST error reduction after removing Type 4-2 is approximately 89%.

claims.text: LST accuracy gain after removing all irregulars is 1.22 points.
claims.poster_quote: LST rises from 97.73% to 99.75%: a 2.02-point gain and approximately 89% error reduction, versus a 1.22-point gain after removing all irregulars.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the LST system, removing only Type 4-2 yields the largest observed gain ... The gain is substantially larger than removing all irregular verbs (+1.22).
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 6 confirm that the LST accuracy gain after removing all irregulars is 1.22 points.

claims.text: PGT accuracy rises from 97.98% to 98.98% after removing Type 4-2.
claims.poster_quote: PGT rises from 97.98% to 98.98%, its best single removal and slightly better than removing all irregulars.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the PGT system, removing Type 4-2 alone is still the single best condition (97.98% → 98.98%).
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 7 confirm that PGT accuracy rises from 97.98% to 98.98% after removing Type 4-2.

claims.text: PGT accuracy gain after removing Type 4-2 is its best single removal.
claims.poster_quote: PGT rises from 97.98% to 98.98%, its best single removal and slightly better than removing all irregulars.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the PGT system, removing Type 4-2 alone is still the single best condition.
claims.reason: Section 6.7 explicitly states that removing Type 4-2 yields the best single removal accuracy gain for PGT.

claims.text: PGT accuracy gain after removing Type 4-2 is slightly better than removing all irregulars.
claims.poster_quote: PGT rises from 97.98% to 98.98%, its best single removal and slightly better than removing all irregulars.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the PGT system, removing Type 4-2 alone is still the single best condition ... the margin over alternative ablations is small.
claims.reason: Section 6.7 confirms that the PGT accuracy gain after removing Type 4-2 is slightly better than removing all irregulars.

claims.text: Removing all irregulars is never optimal.
claims.poster_quote: Removing all irregulars is never optimal; in LST, retaining Types 4-1 and 4-3 is best, while removing 4-1 and 4-2 reaches 99.74%.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: In both systems, removing the full irregular set (Type 4) never yields the maximal accuracy.
claims.reason: Section 6.7 explicitly states that removing all irregulars is never optimal.

claims.text: In LST, retaining Types 4-1 and 4-3 is best for accuracy.
claims.poster_quote: Removing all irregulars is never optimal; in LST, retaining Types 4-1 and 4-3 is best, while removing 4-1 and 4-2 reaches 99.74%.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the LST system, removing only Type 4-2 while retaining 4-1 and 4-3 (condition −4-2) achieves 99.75%.
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 7 confirm that retaining Types 4-1 and 4-3 is best for LST accuracy.

claims.text: In LST, removing Types 4-1 and 4-2 reaches 99.74% accuracy.
claims.poster_quote: Removing all irregulars is never optimal; in LST, retaining Types 4-1 and 4-3 is best, while removing 4-1 and 4-2 reaches 99.74%.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the LST system, removing only Type 4-2 while retaining 4-1 and 4-3 (condition −4-2) achieves 99.75%, and additionally removing 4-1 as well (condition −4-1,4-2) performs nearly as well at 99.74%.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that removing Types 4-1 and 4-2 achieves 99.74% accuracy for the LST system. This is found in Section 6.7, Table 7, and the accompanying text.

claims.text: Each ablation ran once; multi-seed replication is needed.
claims.poster_quote: Each ablation ran once; multi-seed replication is needed.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: First, our ablation experiments were each run once per condition; replication across multiple training runs would strengthen the causal claim.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that each ablation experiment was run once per condition and that multi-seed replication is needed. This is found in the Limitations section.

claims.text: Evidence covers Japanese only, one paradigm, and two Transformers.
claims.poster_quote: Evidence covers Japanese only, one paradigm, and two Transformers.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Second, our study focuses on a single language, a single morphological paradigm, and two Transformer-based architectures.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the evidence is limited to Japanese, one morphological paradigm, and two Transformer-based architectures. This is found in the Limitations section.

claims.text: Ablations identify Type 4-2’s causal role but cannot separate frequency from structural complexity.
claims.poster_quote: Ablations identify Type 4-2’s causal role but cannot separate frequency from structural complexity.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Our analysis is correlational with respect to the specific mechanism (frequency vs. structural complexity vs. their interaction) underlying Type 4-2’s distinctiveness; the ablation results support a causal role for this subtype’s presence in training data, but do not isolate frequency from structural complexity as independent factors.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that the ablation results support a causal role for Type 4-2 but cannot separate frequency from structural complexity. This is found in the Limitations section.

claims.text: Frequency-matched comparisons and alternative representations such as IPA or romanization are needed to isolate the source of difficulty.
claims.poster_quote: Use frequency-matched comparisons and alternative representations such as IPA or romanization to isolate the source of difficulty.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We leave controlled frequency-matched comparisons, and evaluation under alternative input representations (e.g., IPA or romanization), to future work.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly mentions the need for frequency-matched comparisons and alternative representations such as IPA or romanization to isolate the source of difficulty. This is found in the Limitations section.

claims.text: Future work will test whether structural confusability generalizes.
claims.poster_quote: Future work will test whether structural confusability generalizes.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Future work will test whether the Disparity Ratio metric generalizes beyond Japanese to other morphologically rich languages, testing whether structural confusability constitutes a domain-general constraint on morphological learning.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that future work will test whether structural confusability generalizes. This is found in the Discussion section.

claims.text: Future work will evaluate whether large language models overcome Type 4-2 sensitivity through scale.
claims.poster_quote: Evaluate whether large language models overcome Type 4-2 sensitivity through scale. This tests whether the observed inductive bias persists at scale.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: First, whether the same effect appears when models are evaluated zero-shot at scale, testing whether frontier language models show the same Type 4-2 sensitivity or whether scale eliminates the inductive bias.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that future work will evaluate whether large language models overcome Type 4-2 sensitivity through scale. This is found in the Discussion section.

claims.text: Future work will apply Disparity Ratio and subgroup analysis across morphologically rich languages to test domain-general constraints.
claims.poster_quote: Apply Disparity Ratio and subgroup analysis across morphologically rich languages to test domain-general constraints.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Future work will test whether the Disparity Ratio metric generalizes beyond Japanese to other morphologically rich languages, testing whether structural confusability constitutes a domain-general constraint on morphological learning.
claims.reason: The paper explicitly states that future work will apply Disparity Ratio and subgroup analysis across morphologically rich languages to test domain-general constraints. This is found in the Discussion section.

claims.text: Comparable failure modes may recur across languages.
claims.poster_quote: Comparable failure modes may recur across languages.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Future work will test whether the Disparity Ratio metric generalizes beyond Japanese to other morphologically rich languages, testing whether structural confusability constitutes a domain-general constraint on morphological learning.
claims.reason: The paper suggests that comparable failure modes may recur across languages by proposing to test whether structural confusability is a domain-general constraint. This is found in the Discussion section.
